doc.title: Ed Polcer interviewed by Monk Rowe, Tarrytown, New York, October 31, 1998

title: Tastes: Condon-style swing and favourite players
summary: College jazz kept him paid and in the Condon-style swing world; he later worked with Wilson, Hackett, Venuti and Goodman, and admired Ruby Braff.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: Well it paid my way through school so I knew it had an economic thing. And Dixieland or New York Swing, Eddie Condon stuff had a resurgence in the ‘50s, and so I stayed with that because it was very popular at all the colleges. And since it was still popular for me, as soon as I graduated college I still gravitated to the Condon kind of guys. I sat in and played and subbed at Condon’s a couple of times. Most of my gigs were — I don’t like the word traditional but I guess it’s so long ago that people call it traditional now. It was really New York Swing. I mean it wasn’t two-beat jazz, it was straight ahead swing. I mean eventually I’d work with all kinds of players: Teddy Wilson, Bobby Hackett, Joe Venuti. It was a good run of really swing music, and then Benny Goodman — eventually Hackett recommended me to him, so I played with Goodman for nearly a year but that was later on. My tastes? I gravitated from early listening to Wild Bill Davison with the Condon band but then I got to like Bobby Hackett and of course I got to know Bobby Hackett because we played together quite often at some of the things I promoted in Jersey, and people like Buck Clayton. I guess my hero, who I gravitated toward most was Ruby Braff and sort of that middle swing; semi-modern but still good solid swing. And that’s where I gravitated and that’s where I still prefer to be, in that kind of pocket there.
